newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIMEX crude market dealt blow by New York-London link.
newsitem.headline: SIMEX crude market dealt blow by New York-London link.

text.p: Asia's two-year old Brent crude futures market has been dealt a major psychological blow at the hands of global market giants in New York and London, market sources said on Wednesday.

The president of the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) told Reuters in New York on Tuesday he was in talks with London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) about a joint electronic trading system, which would quote the IPE's Brent alongside NYMEX contracts, to help cut trading costs.
Market sources said the news raised questions about the viability of trading Brent on SIMEX and whether the IPE's support for having its Brent contract traded in Singapore was waning.
"It all sounds pretty ominous," one senior broker said. "It would let the IPE off the hook from promoting an open-outcry market for the Brent contract out here."

The IPE has also asked SIMEX to cut its daily trading sessions by 30 minutes so the IPE can open early, further raising doubts about the IPE's support for SIMEX Brent. The IPE says it loses 1,500 lots of business by not opening earlier.
Brent crude oil, produced in the North Sea in Europe, is regarded by the energy industry as the most international crude in the world and therefore the best commodity for hedging.
Brent futures contracts are cash settled, rather than leading to delivery of crude oil, which gives the contract wider appeal for hedging, brokers said.
The IPE agreed for SIMEX to operate a Brent market in Singapore during Asian hours from 1995, to complement trading in London.
The five-year deal expires in 2000 but brokers said the IPE's latest action suggests -- contractual commitments aside -- that its support for trading the crude on SIMEX is waning.
SIMEX officials declined to comment, but an IPE spokeswoman on Tuesday said the IPE had no intention of pulling out of its five-year pact.

SIMEX's Brent market has been dogged since its start with poor trading volumes. It rarely achieves daily volumes of more than a couple of hundred lots, while IPE trades 40,000 to 50,000 lots each day.
"How damaging can the news be when only a few lots are being traded. You have to be realistic. How much business will SIMEX lose," a senior broker said.
"At the end of the day, if traders do not give SIMEX support, which they are not doing, you cannot do anything about it," the senior broker said.
SIMEX market fees are currently cheaper than in London but the NYMEX/IPE tie-up plans would make trading between the two markets cheaper, Thompson said.
But brokers said the low volume of trading on SIMEX was not reflective of a lack of interest in Asia to trade Brent.
Most Brent trading is done in London hours because most physical trading is done in London. If 1,500 lots of extra trading could be done if London opened earlier, they could equally be done on SIMEX.

"It's not a failure of SIMEX Brent that big volume is only traded late afternoon (Asian time). It's basically the way physical markets trade," he said. "As Asia gets bigger voice on physical markets, it will determine its own prices more."
"When the IPE opens does not matter. People will do what they have to do in the time they are permitted," the broker said.
In addition, an open-cry market is more visible and attracts local dealers to make a market on quiet days.
"Put Brent onto the screen and you will lose those quotes," a broker said.
Asia consumes about 17.5 million barrels of crude each day and is likely to rely increasingly on Middle East and West African crudes, which in pricing terms are related to Brent.
